entry.title: Tell them what you noticed
entry.summary: Specific words can share your interest: a line on the page, a careful movement, or the help your child offered. Davies also makes room for your own delight.
entry.cue: Your child looks to you after doing something, or you want to acknowledge their effort.
detail: The book suggests describing the action instead of giving it a general grade. A warm “I’m excited for you” is among Davies’s examples; this is not a rule to hide affection.
She distinguishes an action from a fixed identity. Describing what happened today leaves more room than calling a child “the clever one,” “the clumsy one,” or “the shy one.”
During absorbed activity, you can wait until the child seeks a response rather than interrupting every step.

references.section: Give our child feedback / Roles and labels
references.locator: Specific action descriptions, expressed warmth, action-level words and fixed labels
Wait during concentration, respond when child looks for feedback

ageContext.bookAge: No fixed age; the feedback and label discussion addresses toddlers.
ageContext.readiness: The child looks for a response, or an adult wants to share what they noticed.
ageContext.note: Age and readiness sources: The Montessori Toddler, PDF pp. 14.

displayContext.footer: You don’t need a different home. Start with what you have.
displayContext.colophon: Original summaries inspired by The Montessori Baby and The Montessori Toddler. Open any idea for its book references. The illustration is an invitation to explore, rather than a room to reproduce. Follow your child’s pace.
